newsitem.title: FRANCE: France spawns labour unrest, short of snowballing.
newsitem.headline: France spawns labour unrest, short of snowballing.

text.p: To the outside world, France looks like a hotbed of labour unrest, where truckers block highways, rail workers are always on the warpath and even bank employees take their boss hostage to fight for jobs or better conditions.

It is true to an extent, except that the state of almost perpetual protest in the past year has failed to precipitate the momentum of the rail and public sector strikes which crippled France in late 1995.

While measuring the risk of a repeat is a task which makes many forecasters uncomfortable -- many failed to predict it last time -- the past year of record unemployment and low morale has failed to snowball into the generalised protest and resistance seen in November and December 1995.

An important test comes on Thursday with a one-day rail strike called by the Communist-led CGT and the Socialist CFDT unions, which say that debt-reduction plans involving splitting the SNCF state railways threatens the rail service monopoly and jobs.

Their protest follows a strike last Friday at regional public transport companies in pursuit of a shorter week and early retirement and comes the same week as a protest rally by state and semi-state bank staff for a moratorium on job cuts.

They also coincide with a sit-in at the Paris headquarters of the Credit Foncier bank, where employees and unions fighting to halt government plans to break up the institution held the chairman and board members inside the building for six days at the outset.
One thing is clear, whether it comes from trade unions or interventions from certain politicians in parliament.

Confronted with record 12.7 percent unemployment, people are increasingly immune to government promises that renewed economic growth will bring jobs and that spending cuts are a priority in the meantime to clean up the public deficit and finances.
"This is 1788. French society is on the eve of rebellion," Charles Pasqua, a heavyweight member of the Gaullist governing RPR party of President Jacques Chirac said back in November.

"I believe we're witnessing a change in the way wage-earners behave. They've had enough of working, they're demobilised. They just want to pack their bags and go home," Marc Blondel, leader of the Force Ouvriere (Workers Force) union, said recently after Chirac ruled out the idea of retiring at 55 instead of 60.
The apocalyptic visions of the unionist and the politician look overdone but they do point to the disillusion which Chirac has himself dubbed France's unwarranted "morale deficit".

Equally it is possible to say the government has weathered some of the worst, and that there are few signs of the resolve or solidarity which bound the resistance in late 1995 to Prime Minister Alain Juppe's overhaul of the welfare system.

Union divisions, exacerbated when the CFDT decided to go along with Juppe's welfare reforms, run deep and the debate still rages over whether they should stick to protest platforms, like the CGT and Force Ouvriere, or opt to work from within the system, a direction taken by CFDT leader Nicole Notat.
The government has dropped the plans to end early retirement for railworkers, the catalyst for the strikes last time round.

Six minority unions have signed up its latest rail reforms. Even if the CGT and CFDT orchestrate an effective strike this week, their campaign is about a less immediate issue and harder to sell to a public which proved highly tolerant last time.

Cutbacks in the civil service and state teaching staff under the 1997 budget provoked a public sector strike on October 17, which was a moderate success but has since failed to develop much further, although pay talks after a wage freeze in 1996 could raise the tempo once again.

And the government has yet to see whether plans for the creation of private pension funds, universally condemned by unions on the grounds that incentives for employers will undermine the current state pensions system, will add fuel to the flames.
